summary:
Orbit ZA (Earth Speaks) is an interactive web application that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar observations into warnings people can actually use. Users choose a place, find NISAR observations, compare two dates, and see where the surface has changed, such as expanding water along the Umgeni River in Durban, South Africa. The app then overlays nearby settlements, clinics, schools and roads to check who is exposed, and offers a clearly labelled digital-twin flood scenario over the next 1 to 24 hours. Alerts are designed to reach everyone: through Orbit Lights streetlights, solar message signs for people without phones, SMS for basic phones, and community hubs.

This addresses the challenge by making radar-observed surface change easy to visualise, understand and communicate. It matters because the gap is not data, it is translation: the 2022 KwaZulu-Natal floods killed 443 people, yet warnings often do not reach informal settlements. Every layer is labelled observed, derived, modelled or simulated, so the prototype stays honest about what it proves.
details:
What it does and how it works
Orbit ZA (Earth Speaks) is an interactive web application that turns NASA-ISRO NISAR radar observations into warnings people can actually use. A user chooses a place, and the app searches for NISAR observations, listing real acquisition dates, or clearly saying when none exist. The user picks an earlier and a later observation and compares them with a swipe view. The app then applies a method suited to the data (radar backscatter change, water extent, or ground displacement from suitable InSAR products) and explains what the result measures and what it cannot prove. Next it overlays nearby settlements, clinics, schools, roads and rivers to show who may be exposed. A digital twin then shows a clearly labelled, modelled flood scenario over 1 to 24 hours. Our demonstration area is the Umgeni River floodplain in Durban, South Africa.

Benefits and intended impact
The gap is not data, it is translation. Satellite and rainfall data stay with experts, while communities in informal settlements often receive late or no warnings. We aim to make radar-observed change easy to see and understand, and to carry authorised alerts to everyone: through streetlights (Orbit Lights, an LED halo while normal lighting stays on), solar variable message signs for people without phones, SMS for basic or incompatible phones (through planned mobile-network partnerships), and radio and community hubs such as schools, clinics and churches.

Tools and data
NASA-ISRO NISAR radar (found via the Alaska Satellite Facility) is our primary source. Context data includes NASA GPM IMERG rainfall, SMAP soil moisture, SRTM/NASADEM terrain and OpenStreetMap facilities, with NASA FIRMS planned for fire. The prototype is a web app hosted on Vercel, with a map interface and an SVG streetlight visual. [Add your coding languages, frameworks and libraries here.] No special hardware is needed for the prototype; streetlights and solar signs are virtual. Real deployment would use connected streetlight controllers, solar signs and SMS through mobile networks.

What makes it creative
We treat the problem as translation, not mapping. Orbit Lights reuses existing streetlights, and the solar signs and SMS reach people with no phone or a basic one. Every layer is labelled Observed, Derived, Modelled or Simulated, so users always know what is real.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: deaf, blind and elderly residents, and people with basic phones or little data.
  • Satellite limits: NISAR is not a live feed (nominal 12-day cycle), so we show real acquisition dates.
  • Scientific honesty: backscatter change is not ground movement, and a digital twin is a scenario, not a forecast.
  • Safety: two-source checks, human approval for Red alerts, and official warnings staying with authorised agencies.
  • Plan: a phased pilot validated with communities
